name: C Programming & Systems Engineering Track
description: Master low-level programming in C: Pointers, manual memory allocation (malloc/free), structs, bitwise operations, file handling, and systems software architecture.
whatYouLearn: Understand C memory layout (Stack vs Heap)
Master pointer arithmetic, dereferencing, and memory addresses
Allocate and free heap memory manually (malloc, calloc, realloc, free)
Define custom data structures using structs and typedefs
Manipulate binary data with bitwise operators (&, |, ^, ~, <<, >>)
Build a production Bank Management System CLI

exercises.title: C Program Structure & printf Formats
exercises.description: Write a C program with main(), include headers, and format printf outputs.
exercises.theory: C programs begin execution at main(). Include <stdio.h> for standard I/O functions and specify format specifiers (%d, %f, %s, %p) in printf().
exercises.objective: Write a C program using printf with formatted specifiers.
requirements: Include <stdio.h>
Declare int, double, and char variables
Use %d, %.2f, and %c format specifiers in printf
Return 0 from main()
hints: %.2f formats floating point numbers to 2 decimal places

exercises.title: Variable Types & Memory Sizes (sizeof operator)
exercises.description: Determine byte memory allocation size for primitive C types using sizeof.
exercises.theory: The sizeof operator returns the byte size of data types or variables in memory at compile time.
exercises.objective: Print byte sizes of int, float, double, char, and pointers.
requirements: Use sizeof() for char, int, float, double, and int*
Use %zu format specifier for size_t values
hints: Pointers take 8 bytes on 64-bit operating systems

exercises.title: Pointers & Memory Address Operator (&, *)
exercises.description: Store memory addresses in pointer variables and dereference values.
exercises.theory: The address-of operator (&) gets an element's memory location address. The dereference operator (*) accesses or mutates the value stored at that address.
exercises.objective: Declare a pointer variable and mutate data via pointer dereferencing.
requirements: Declare int *ptr = &val
Print memory address using %p format specifier
Mutate val by assigning value to *ptr
hints: *ptr = 250 writes directly to the memory address stored in ptr

exercises.title: Pass-by-Reference via Pointers in Functions
exercises.description: Modify function argument variables in caller scope using pointer arguments.
exercises.theory: C passes parameters by value (copying data). To allow a function to modify caller variables, pass memory address pointers.
exercises.objective: Write a swap() function using pointer parameters.
requirements: Write void swap(int *x, int *y)
Use temporary variable inside swap
Pass addresses &a and &b when calling swap()
hints: Pass address &a to match parameter pointer int *x
exercises.codeExample: void swap(int *a, int *b) { int t = *a; *a = *b; *b = t; }

exercises.title: Arrays & Pointer Arithmetic
exercises.description: Traverse array items using pointer arithmetic (*(ptr + i)).
exercises.theory: An array name in C decays into a pointer to its first element (&arr[0]). arr[i] is equivalent to *(arr + i).
exercises.objective: Traverse array using pointer offset arithmetic.
requirements: Assign pointer ptr to array base numbers
Traverse array elements using *(ptr + i) pointer arithmetic
hints: Adding 1 to an int* pointer advances the memory address by sizeof(int) bytes (usually 4 bytes)

exercises.title: Strings & Null Terminators ('\0')
exercises.description: Manipulate C character arrays ending with the null terminator character ('\0').
exercises.theory: Strings in C are char arrays terminated by a null character ('\0'). <string.h> provides utility functions (strlen, strcpy, strcmp).
exercises.objective: Calculate string length manually using pointer traversal.
exercises.initialCode:
#include <stdio.h>

// Write string length function
requirements: Traverse char pointer until null terminator '\0'
Return string character count
hints: Pointer subtraction (ptr - str) calculates element count distance between two pointers

exercises.title: Dynamic Memory Allocation: malloc & free
exercises.description: Allocate heap memory dynamically with malloc() and free it with free().
exercises.theory: malloc(bytes) allocates uninitialized heap memory. Always check for NULL allocation failures and call free(ptr) when finished.
exercises.objective: Dynamically allocate integer array on the heap using malloc().
requirements: Include <stdlib.h>
Allocate memory using malloc(n * sizeof(int))
Check if arr == NULL guard
Deallocate with free(arr) and assign NULL
hints: Always set pointer to NULL after calling free() to prevent dangling pointer access

exercises.title: Dynamic Allocation: calloc & realloc
exercises.description: Allocate zero-initialized memory with calloc() and resize memory blocks with realloc().
exercises.theory: calloc(count, size) allocates memory cleared to zero. realloc(ptr, new_size) resizes an existing heap allocation.
exercises.objective: Allocate memory with calloc and expand block using realloc.
requirements: Allocate 3 zero-filled ints with calloc()
Resize to 5 ints with realloc() using temporary pointer guard
Deallocate with free()
hints: Use temporary pointer when calling realloc to prevent memory leaks if realloc returns NULL
exercises.codeExample: int *p = calloc(5, sizeof(int)); p = realloc(p, 10 * sizeof(int));

exercises.title: Structs & Custom Data Types
exercises.description: Define composite data structures using struct and typedef keywords.
exercises.theory: struct groups variables of different types under a single composite type name. typedef creates concise type aliases.
exercises.objective: Define a Student struct with typedef and initialize instances.
requirements: Define typedef struct with id, name[50], and gpa fields
Initialize struct fields using dot notation (s1.id)
Use strcpy for string array assignment
hints: Use strcpy() from <string.h> to assign text to char arrays inside structs
exercises.codeExample: typedef struct { int x; int y; } Point;

exercises.title: Pointers to Structs & Arrow Operator (->)
exercises.description: Access struct members through pointers using the arrow operator (ptr->member).
exercises.theory: When accessing struct fields through a struct pointer, ptr->member is syntactic sugar for (*ptr).member.
exercises.objective: Pass struct pointers to functions and access fields using ->.
exercises.initialCode:
#include <stdio.h>

// Access struct via pointer arrow operator
requirements: Pass struct pointer Point *p to function
Access and mutate fields using p->x and p->y arrow operator syntax
hints: p->x is shorthand for (*p).x

exercises.title: Bitwise Operators (&, |, ^, ~, <<, >>)
exercises.description: Perform binary bitwise manipulations and bit masking operations.
exercises.theory: Bitwise operators operate directly on individual bits: AND (&), OR (|), XOR (^), NOT (~), Left Shift (<<), Right Shift (>>).
exercises.objective: Toggle and test specific bit flags using bit masks.
requirements: Use bit shift 1 << n to create bit masks
Set bit using OR (|=) and test bit using AND (&)
hints: flags |= MASK sets a bit to 1; flags &= ~MASK clears a bit to 0

exercises.title: File I/O: Reading & Writing Text Files (fopen, fprintf, fgets)
exercises.description: Open text files and execute I/O operations using FILE pointers.
exercises.theory: File I/O uses FILE pointers returned by fopen(filename, mode). Always check for NULL and close handles with fclose(file).
exercises.objective: Write text lines to a file and read them back line-by-line using fgets().
requirements: Open file with mode 'w' and write lines with fprintf
Open file with mode 'r' and read lines with fgets in a loop
Close file handles with fclose(fp)
hints: fgets returns NULL when reaching end-of-file (EOF)

exercises.title: Binary File I/O (fread, fwrite)
exercises.description: Read and write raw binary struct records directly using fread and fwrite.
exercises.theory: fwrite and fread stream raw bytes of struct records directly to disk in binary mode ('wb' / 'rb').
exercises.objective: Write a struct record to a binary file and read it back.
exercises.initialCode:
#include <stdio.h>

// Write struct to binary file
requirements: Open file in binary modes 'wb' and 'rb'
Use fwrite(&record, sizeof(Record), 1, fp)
Use fread(&record, sizeof(Record), 1, fp)
hints: Binary mode preserves raw byte representations without line-ending translation

exercises.title: Function Pointers
exercises.description: Declare function pointers and pass functions as arguments to callbacks.
exercises.theory: Function pointers store memory addresses of executable functions, enabling callback patterns and dispatch tables in C.
exercises.objective: Declare function pointer syntax and pass to a process_array callback function.
exercises.initialCode:
#include <stdio.h>

// Declare function pointer callback
requirements: Declare function pointer type int (*op)(int, int)
Pass add and multiply functions to compute callback runner
hints: Function pointer syntax requires parentheses around (*ptr_name)

exercises.title: Singly Linked List Data Structure
exercises.description: Implement a Singly Linked List with dynamic Node allocation and traversal.
exercises.theory: A Linked List is a dynamic linear data structure composed of nodes. Each node contains a data payload and a pointer to the next node.
exercises.objective: Build insert_head and print_list functions for a linked list.
requirements: Define Node struct with data and struct Node *next pointer
Write insert_head allocating new node on heap
Traverse and print list
hints: Double pointer Node **head allows updating the caller's head pointer
exercises.codeExample: typedef struct Node { int data; struct Node *next; } Node;

exercises.title: Command-Line Arguments (argc, argv)
exercises.description: Parse command-line flags and parameters passed to main(int argc, char *argv[]).
exercises.theory: argc is the argument count integer. argv is an array of null-terminated C string argument pointers.
exercises.objective: Parse command line arguments in main.
requirements: Use signature int main(int argc, char *argv[])
Iterate over argv array starting from index 1
hints: argv[0] always contains the program executable invocation name
exercises.codeExample: int main(int argc, char *argv[]) { printf("%s", argv[0]); }

exercises.title: Unions & Memory Sharing
exercises.description: Store different data types in the same shared memory location using union.
exercises.theory: Unions allow storing different data types in a single shared memory location. Size of union equals the size of its largest member.
exercises.objective: Declare a Data union and inspect member memory sharing.
exercises.initialCode:
#include <stdio.h>

// Declare Data union
requirements: Declare typedef union Data containing int, float, and char array
Inspect sizeof(Data)
hints: Assigning a new union member overwrites previous member data values
exercises.codeExample: union Val { int i; float f; };

exercises.title: Volatile & Register Keywords
exercises.description: Control compiler optimization using volatile and register type qualifiers.
exercises.theory: volatile informs the compiler that a variable value can change unexpectedly (e.g. hardware interrupt), disabling aggressive optimization.
exercises.objective: Declare volatile hardware status variable.
requirements: Declare volatile int hardware_status
Declare register int fast_counter
hints: volatile prevents compiler from caching variable values in CPU registers

exercises.title: C Preprocessor Directives (#define, #ifdef, Macros)
exercises.description: Define macros, conditional compilation guards, and inline function macros.
exercises.theory: The preprocessor runs before compilation. Use #define for constants/macros and #ifdef/#ifndef for header include guards.
exercises.objective: Write macro functions MAX(a, b) and conditional compilation guards.
exercises.initialCode:
#include <stdio.h>

// Write macro directives
requirements: Define macro constant PLATFORM
Define parameterized macro MAX(a, b) with protective parentheses
Use #ifdef conditional compilation block
hints: Always enclose macro parameter arguments in parentheses ((a) > (b)) to avoid precedence bugs

exercises.title: Capstone Project: Bank Account Management System CLI
exercises.description: Build a production-grade Bank Management System featuring Structs, Pointers, Dynamic Memory Allocation (malloc/realloc), and Binary File Persistence.
exercises.theory: This capstone project synthesizes C systems programming: Structs, pointer manipulation, manual memory management (malloc/realloc/free), binary file I/O (fread/fwrite), and modular functions.
exercises.objective: Construct a complete Bank Account Management System module.
exercises.initialCode: // Construct Bank Management System CLI Engine
requirements: Define Account and BankSystem structs
Implement init_bank, add_account with realloc expansion, and free_bank
Deallocate heap memory cleanly with free()
hints: Multiply capacity by 2 when bank->count reaches capacity, then call realloc
exercises.codeExample: typedef struct { Account *arr; int count; } Bank;

references.title: C Programming Language (ANSI C ISO/IEC 9899)
references.description: Authoritative specification for standard C language and standard library headers
